source_text: Προφανεῖς μὲν οὖν καὶ πᾶσαι αἱ ἄλλαι ἀρεταί, αἱ παρὰ τῷ Μωυσεῖ ἀναγεγραμμέναι, ἀρχὴν Ἕλλησι παντὸς τοῦ ἠθικοῦ τόπου παρασχόμεναι, ἀνδρείαν λέγω καὶ σωφροσύνην καὶ φρόνησιν καὶ δικαιοσύνην καρτερίαν τε καὶ ὑπομονὴν καὶ τὴν σεμνότητα καὶ ἐγκράτειαν τήν τε ἐπὶ τούτοις εὐσέβειαν. ἀλλ’ ἡ μὲν εὐσέβεια παντί που δήλη τὸ ἀνωτάτω καὶ πρεσβύτατον αἴτιον σέβειν καὶ τιμᾶν καὶ διδάσκουσα. καὶ δικαιοσύνην δὲ αὐτὸς ὁ νόμος παρίστησι παιδεύων τήν τε φρόνησιν διὰ τῆς τῶν αἰσθητῶν εἰδώλων ἀποχῆς καὶ τῆς πρὸς τὸν ποιητὴν καὶ πατέρα τῶν ὅλων προσκληρώσεως, ἀφ’ ἧς δόξης οἷον πηγῆς πᾶσα σύνεσις αὔξεται. θυσίαι γὰρ ἀνόμων βδέλυγμα κυρίῳ, εὐχαὶ δὲ κατευθυνόντων δεκταὶ παρ’ αὐτῷ. ἐπεὶ οιαῦτα καὶ τὰ παρὰ Ἡσαΐᾳ· τί μοι πλῆθος τῶν θυσιῶν ὑμῶν ὑμῶν; λέγει κύριος, καὶ πᾶσα ἡ περικοπή· λῦε πάντα σύνδεσμον ἀδικίας· αὕτη γὰρ θυσία θεῷ δεκτή, καρδία συντετριμμένη καὶ ζητοῦσα τὸν πεπλακότα. ζυγὰ δόλια βδέλυγμα ἔναντι θεοῦ, στάθμιον δὲ δίκαιον δεκτὸν αὐτῷ. ἐντεῦθεν ζυγὸν μὴ ὑπερβαίνειν Πυθαγόρας παραινεῖ. δικαιοσύνη δὲ δολία εἴρηται ἡ τῶν αἱρέσεων ἐπαγγελία, καὶ γλῶσσα μὲν ἀδίκων ἐξολεῖται, στόμα δὲ δικαίων ἀποστάζει σοφίαν. ἀλλὰ γὰρ τοὺς σοφοὺς καὶ φρονίμους φαύλους καλοῦσιν. μακρὸν δ’ ἂν εἴη περὶ τῶν ἀρετῶν τούτων μαρτυρίας παρατίθεσθαι, ἁπάσης ταύτας ἐξυμνούσης τῆς γραφῆς. ἐπεὶ δ’ οὖν τὴν μὲν ἀνδρείαν ὁρίζονται ἐπιστήμην δεινῶν καὶ οὐ δεινῶν καὶ τῶν μεταξύ, τὴν δὲ σωφροσύνην ἕξιν ἐν αἱρέσει καὶ φυγῇ σῴζουσαν τὰ τῆς φρονήσεως κρίματα, παράκειται τε τῇ μὲν ἀνδρείᾳ ἥ τε ὑπομονή, ἣν καρτερίαν καλοῦσιν, ἐπιστήμην ἐμμενετέων καὶ οὐκ ἐμμενετέων, ἥ τε μεγαλοψυχία, ἐπιστήμη τῶν συμβαινόντων ὑπεραίρουσα, ἀλλὰ καὶ τῇ σωφροσύνῃ ἡ εὐλάβεια, ἔκκλισις οὖσα σὺν λόγῳ. Φυλακὴ δὲ τῶν ἐντολῶν, τήρησις οὖσα αὐτῶν ἀβλαβής, περιποίησίς ἐστιν ἀσφαλείας βίου. καὶ οὐκ ἔστιν ἄνευ ἀνδρείας καρτερικὸν εἶναι οὐδὲ μὴν ἄνευ σωφροσύνης ἐγκρατῆ. ἀντακολουθοῦσι δὲ ἀλλήλαις αἱ ἀρεταί, καἰ παρ’ ᾧ αἱ τῶν ἀρετῶν ἀκολουθίαι, παρὰ τούτῳ καὶ ἡ σωτηρία, τήρησις οὖσα τοῦ εὖ ἔχοντος. εἰκότως ἔτι περὶ τούτων διαλαβόντες τῶν ἀρετῶν περὶ πασῶν ἂν εἴημεν ἐσκεμμένοι, ὅτι ὁ μίαν ἔχων ἀρετὴν γνωστικῶς πάσας ἔχει διὰ τὴν ἀντακολουθίαν. αὐτίκα ἡ ἐγκράτεια διάθεσίς ἐστιν ἀνυπέρβατος τῶν κατὰ τὸν ὀρθὸν λόγον φανέντων. ἐγκρατεύεται δὲ ὁ κατέχων τὰς παρὰ τὸν ὀρθὸν λόγον ὁρμὰς ἢ ὁ κατέχων αὑτὸν ὥστε μὴ ὁρμᾶν παρὰ τὸν ὀρθὸν λόγον. σωφροσύνη δὲ αὕτη οὐκ ἄνευ ἀνδρείας, ἐπειδὴ ἐξ ἐντολῶν γίνεται ἑπομένη τῷ διατεταγμένῳ θεῷ φρόνησίς τε καὶ ἡ μιμητικὴ τῆς θείας διαθέσεως δικαιοσύνη, καθ’ ἣν ἐγκρατευόμενοι καθαροὶ πρὸς εὐσέβειαν καὶ τὴν ἑπομένην ἀκολούθως τῷ θεῷ πρᾶξιν στελλόμεθα, ἐξομοιούμενοι τῷ κυρίῳ κατὰ τὸ δυνατὸν ἡμῖν, ἐπικήροις τὴν φύσιν ὑπάρχουσιν.
pass_a_gloss: The other virtues, which are written by Moses, are evident and provide a starting point for all ethical matters for the Greeks, including courage and self-control and prudence and justice and patience and perseverance and dignity and self-control and the piety that is based on these. But piety is evident to everyone as the highest and most ancient cause to reverence and honor and teach. The law itself also presents justice, teaching prudence through the avoidance of sensory idols and the calling towards the creator and father of all, from which glory, as if from a source, all understanding increases. For sacrifices of the lawless are an abomination to the Lord, but the prayers of those who are guided are acceptable to Him. Since also the things from Isaiah say: what is the multitude of your sacrifices to me, says the Lord, and the whole passage says: loose every bond of injustice, for this is a sacrifice acceptable to God, a heart that is broken and seeking the one who has been afflicted. False balances are an abomination before God, but a just scale is acceptable to Him. From this, Pythagoras advises not to exceed the balance. Justice, however, is said to be false, the promise of the sects, and the tongue of the unrighteous will be destroyed, but the mouth of the righteous will overflow with wisdom. But they call the wise and prudent ones worthless. It would be long to present testimonies about these virtues, which the whole scripture praises. Since, then, they define courage as the knowledge of what is fearful and not fearful and what is in between, and self-control as a state that saves the judgments of prudence in choice and avoidance, perseverance, which they call patience, is placed beside courage, as the knowledge of what is to be endured and not to be endured, and magnanimity, as the knowledge of what happens, surpassing it. But also caution is placed beside self-control, as a withdrawal with reason. The guarding of the commandments, being the blameless keeping of them, is the acquisition of the security of life. And it is not possible to be patient without courage or self-controlled without self-control. The virtues follow one another, and where the sequences of the virtues are, there also is salvation, being the keeping of what is good. It is reasonable, then, that having taken up these virtues, we would be concerned with all of them, because the one who has one virtue knowingly has all of them through their sequence. Immediately, self-control is a disposition that is unsurpassed regarding the things that appear according to the right reason. Self-control is exercised by the one who holds back the impulses that are contrary to the right reason or by the one who holds himself back so as not to be impelled contrary to the right reason. But self-control is not without courage, since it comes from the commandments and follows the God who has been ordained, and prudence and the justice that imitates the divine disposition, according to which, being self-controlled, we are pure towards piety and the action that follows God, being conformed to the Lord as much as possible, having a nature that is subordinate.

choices.why: The verb ἐγκρατεύεται means to exercise self-control.
The noun ἐπιστήμη means knowledge or science.
The verb ἐξομοιούμενοι means to be conformed or made like.

bible_refs.note: The passage from Isaiah is quoted.
The reference to false balances is an allusion to Proverbs 11:1.

pass_b_english: The other virtues recorded by Moses are clear enough, and they gave the Greeks a starting point for the whole field of ethics: courage, self-control, prudence, justice, patience, perseverance, dignity, self-mastery, and the piety that rests on these. Piety, however, is evident to everyone as the highest and most ancient obligation to reverence, honor, and instruct. The law itself also presents justice, teaching prudence through the avoidance of sensory idols and the calling of people toward the Creator and Father of all, from whose glory, as from a source, all understanding grows. For the sacrifices of the lawless are an abomination to the Lord, but the prayers of those who walk rightly are acceptable to Him (Isaiah 1:11-17). Since the same truths appear in Isaiah: "What is the multitude of your sacrifices to me?" says the Lord, and the whole passage continues: "Loose every bond of injustice, for this is a sacrifice acceptable to God, a heart that is broken and seeking the one who has been afflicted." False balances are an abomination before God, but a just scale is acceptable to Him (Proverbs 11:1). From this, Pythagoras advises not to exceed the balance. Yet the promise of the sects is called false justice; the tongue of the unrighteous will be destroyed, but the mouth of the righteous will overflow with wisdom. They even call the wise and prudent worthless. It would take too long to lay out testimonies about these virtues, since all of Scripture sings their praise.

Since, then, they define courage as the knowledge of what is fearful, what is not, and what lies between, and self-control as a state that preserves the judgments of prudence in choice and avoidance, perseverance—which they call patience—stands alongside courage as the knowledge of what must be endured and what must not, and magnanimity stands there as the knowledge that rises above whatever happens. Caution, too, stands alongside self-control as a reasoned withdrawal. The keeping of the commandments, which is their blameless observance, is the securing of a safe life. It is not possible to be patient without courage, nor self-controlled without self-control. The virtues follow one another, and where the sequences of the virtues are found, there also is salvation, which is the keeping of what is good. It is reasonable, then, that having engaged with these virtues we would be versed in all of them, because the one who possesses one virtue knowingly possesses them all through their interconnection. At once, self-control is a disposition that cannot be surpassed in the things that appear according to right reason. One exercises self-control either by restraining impulses contrary to right reason or by restraining oneself so as not to be driven contrary to right reason. Yet self-control is not without courage, since it arises from the commandments and follows the God who has ordained them—along with prudence and the justice that imitates the divine disposition—by which, as we exercise self-control, we are made pure toward piety and toward the action that follows God accordingly, being conformed to the Lord as far as we can, since we possess a nature that is subordinate.
